Algorithmic Authority and Information Calibration
How generative AI changes additional search and belief updating under uncertainty

text: Problem shift
The question is not only what answer AI gives. The question is whether AI changes when people feel ready to stop looking for more evidence.

text: Dissertation position
Paper 1 studies the first link in the broader chain: how AI reshapes the move from evidence to belief.
textPreview: Paper 1 studies the first link in the broader chain: how AI reshapes the move from evidence to belief.

text: Belief formation -> reliance calibration -> responsibility

This first paper focuses on the opening step in the dissertation: how AI changes the movement from evidence to belief.
The key shift is that generative AI does not just give a faster answer. It may change when users feel they have already seen enough and no longer need additional evidence.
So the central object is information calibration, not the older framing of double Bayesian distortion as a starting theory.

text:
I want to start with a simple and familiar contrast rather than an abstract framework.
In a search-engine setting, users usually see sources first and construct an interpretation later. In an AI-assistant setting, they often receive a coherent interpretation before they have seen the raw evidence.
That reversal is the opening intuition for the whole paper. It suggests that AI may change not just how much people search, but how they judge the value of searching further.

This slide cuts off a common shortcut in the discussion of AI and search.
If users search less after receiving an AI answer, that is not automatically a problem. It could be rational compression if the summary already captures informative evidence.
The paper therefore asks a stricter question: when search falls, do later beliefs still stay close to the appropriate benchmark, or do they move away from it?

text:
Here I want to anchor the paper in the existing literature more concretely.
The image summarizes the closest literature targets on automation bias, reduced search, and verification. These papers are valuable, but they often move too quickly from less search to worse judgment, or they treat verification intensity as the key mechanism.
My paper's move is different. I ask whether AI changes information calibration: whether users still correctly judge the value of additional evidence, and whether posterior quality remains aligned with what they think they know.
TRADITIONAL BENCHMARK
The standard benchmark says people should stop when extra evidence is no longer worth its cost

text:
The traditional benchmark behind this paper is a search-cost benchmark.
People should stop searching when the expected value of additional evidence falls below the cost of getting it. So stopping early is not automatically irrational.
The paper becomes interesting only if AI changes the stopping rule in a way that makes users think the evidence is already sufficient when, in fact, it is not.

text:
This is the gap that motivates the paper.
The unresolved question is not merely whether AI reduces search. It is whether an AI answer changes the user's judgment that the current evidence is already enough.
That matters because a shift in perceived sufficiency can affect later evidence acquisition, later Bayesian updating, and the user's own sense of how much they really know.

text:
At this point I can state the paper's analytical framing directly.
The paper is not about generic AI trust. It is about information calibration: whether users correctly assess if more evidence is still worth acquiring after they receive an answer-first summary.
Algorithmic authority matters here because the AI label can change what users infer about how much searching and integration has already happened behind the scenes.

text:
The paper's mechanism is not that users merely read a conclusion and obey it.
They infer a hidden signal structure behind the summary: that more searching has already occurred, that conflict has already been resolved, and that counterevidence has already been processed.
If those inferences are too strong, then the perceived value of additional evidence can fall too quickly, and that is where harmful under-search becomes possible.
RESEARCH QUESTIONS
The study asks three linked questions

text: RQ1
Does an AI-labeled summary lower the stopping threshold for additional search?

text: RQ2
When search falls, is that rational information compression or harmful information-acquisition deviation?

text: RQ3
Does subjective information mastery become misaligned with objective judgment quality?

text:
The three research questions are deliberately ordered.
The first is behavioral: does the AI label change the stopping threshold for additional search? The second is normative: when search declines, is that efficient compression or harmful deviation? The third is metacognitive: do subjective mastery and objective judgment quality separate from each other?
That sequence is what allows the paper to move from what users do, to whether it is justified, to whether they recognize their own informational position correctly.

Before moving to the full design, I want to explain what the task prototype must accomplish.
It has to hold the initial content constant when the label changes, keep additional search cost the same across conditions, and make the value of each new evidence item calculable.
That is why the paper uses a fixed and controlled evidence environment rather than an open search setting.

This is an important correction relative to the older six-cell description.
The current design has five groups. There is one no-summary baseline that enters the shared full evidence pool directly, and then four summary groups produced by completeness crossed with source label.
The baseline does not need to be split in two, because the baseline always faces the same full pool rather than a separate summary condition.

This slide captures the cleanest identification logic in the design.
The unlabeled-summary and AI-labeled-summary groups read exactly the same summary text. The only difference is whether the source is explicitly marked as AI.
So if their later search, posterior, or mastery judgments diverge, that difference cannot be attributed to content. It has to come from the source label and the authority inferences it triggers.

This slide shows why the experiment can move beyond raw click counts.
Because the evidence pool is fixed and each item has a known likelihood ratio, we can compute the posterior that should follow from the evidence a participant actually saw.
That gives the paper a normative benchmark and lets it compare behavioral search depth with informational quality rather than confusing the two.

It identifies cases such as seeing less but updating well, seeing more but updating badly, and seeing too little because evidentiary sufficiency was overestimated.
textPreview: It identifies cases such as seeing less but updating well, seeing more but updating badly, and seeing too little because evidentiary suff...

text:
This distinction is methodologically central.
Conditional deviation asks whether people used the evidence they actually saw correctly. Full-information deviation asks whether they stopped too early relative to the complete pool.
That is what allows the paper to separate harmful under-search from poor updating instead of treating all posterior error as one undifferentiated mistake.

The paper expects subjective mastery, confidence, and epistemic ownership to become separable from objective posterior quality.

text:
The paper's third contribution is metacognitive rather than purely behavioral.
Direct search can produce stronger epistemic ownership because the user did the work personally, but that does not necessarily produce a better posterior. Summary use can produce a better posterior while still leaving the user with a weaker sense of ownership.
So one expected pattern is an information-calibration mismatch between subjective mastery and objective judgment quality.

text:
The closing idea is that the same behavioral fact, less additional search, can correspond to very different underlying realities.
In one case it reflects efficient compression. In another it reflects harmful under-search because evidentiary sufficiency was overestimated. And in a third layer it may coexist with a mismatch between objective quality and subjective mastery.
That is why the paper's governance implication is not simply to tell people to verify more. It is to understand how AI changes judgments about when further evidence is still worth seeking.
